content:
Dr. Seuss's most famous troublemaker is back in theaters — this time as a cartoon. Warner Bros. Pictures Animation's The Cat in the Hat, the first fully animated theatrical feature built around the character, opened wide Friday, November 6, in roughly 4,000 theaters, with Saturday Night Live and Barry veteran Bill Hader voicing the Cat.

The film, directed and written by Erica Rivinoja and Alessandro Carloni, gives the 1957 picture book a new backstory: the Cat turns up to bring his signature chaotic joy into the lives of two siblings struggling to adjust to a move to a new town. The voice cast also includes Matt Berry as the family fish, Quinta Brunson, Xochitl Gomez, Tiago Martinez, Giancarlo Esposito and America Ferrera. The film is rated PG and runs 91 minutes.

It is the first feature born from Warner Bros.' partnership with Dr. Seuss Enterprises, and the studio's attempt at a clean break from the live-action version that starred Mike Myers in 2003. That film holds an 11 percent score on Rotten Tomatoes; the new one is faring better, but only modestly so.

Critics are split almost down the middle. The animated film holds a 48 percent score on Rotten Tomatoes from 48 critics, and a 47 on Metacritic, which the site rates as "Mixed or Average." The Hollywood Reporter's Frank Scheck called it an improvement on the 2003 version but still "more taxing than enjoyable," while Variety's Owen Gleiberman described it as "junior Marvel surrealism." On the other side, AwardsWatch gave the film 75 out of 100, writing that it "is loud, unruly, and occasionally a little too pleased with its own chaos, but its good humor is hard to resist."

The box office picture looks similarly mixed. Industry watchers expect the film to open in second place this weekend with $20 million to $25 million, behind the kaiju sequel Godzilla Minus Zero, which is tracking at $29 million to $35 million. The Cat's opening would trail the 2003 film's $38.3 million debut — and the new film reportedly cost $92 million to produce, before marketing.

The road to theaters was not smooth, either. The project was first dated for March 6, then pushed to February 27, before Warner Bros. finally settled on November 6. The holiday-season slot gives the film a long runway with family audiences, and history suggests a weak critical reception does not automatically sink a family release built around a recognizable name: the 2003 film finished with $134 million worldwide despite its reviews.

Analysis: A familiar gamble with a familiar name

Warner Bros. is betting that the Cat himself is bigger than any review. The character has sold books for nearly 70 years, and the studio's animated reset — a new voice, a new look, a new story — is designed to let a new generation meet him without the baggage of the 2003 film. The split reviews suggest that reset only partly worked. What will decide the film's fate is not the Tomatometer but the Thanksgiving corridor ahead: family films with soft openings have recovered before when the calendar turns in their favor. If the Cat can hold its audience through the holidays, the $92 million bet pays off. If not, it becomes the latest lesson that a beloved name guarantees an opening weekend, not a hit.

title: The Cat in the Hat Leaps to the Big Screen in Animation — but Critics Are Split on the Seuss Reboot
